title: What is a tide pool?
answer: When the sea goes out, water can stay behind in a hollow in the rocks. That little pocket of seawater is a tide pool. A pool may hold snails, anemones, and other animals even when the rocks around it look dry. These pockets form within the intertidal zone, the strip of shore that tides cover and uncover. Sunshine can warm the trapped water, and rain can make it less salty. The next high tide may wash over the whole pool and bring a fresh supply of seawater.
facts: A tide pool is only one kind of home on a rocky shore. Some shore animals live on exposed rock outside the pools.

title: Where is the intertidal zone?
answer: Stand back from a shore and imagine two lines across it. One marks how high the water reaches at high tide. The other shows how far it drops at low tide. The shore between those lines is the intertidal zone. Animals near the upper line spend more time exposed to air than those near the lower line. Which animals you find can change as you move down the rocks.
facts: An intertidal zone can be a sandy beach or a wide mudflat instead of a rocky slope.

title: How does a barnacle live stuck to a rock?
answer: An acorn barnacle starts life swimming in the sea. Later it settles on a hard surface and sticks there. The adult grows a set of hard plates around its body. When seawater covers it, plates at the top can open. The barnacle sweeps feathery legs out of the opening to catch tiny drifting animals and other plankton. When the shore is exposed, closing the plates helps keep its body from drying out.
facts: A barnacle is a crustacean, in the same large group of animals as crabs and shrimp.

title: How does a limpet hold on to a rock?
answer: A limpet is a sea snail with a shell shaped a little like a low hat. A broad, muscular foot spreads under it. The foot gives the limpet a strong grip when waves wash across a rock. Many limpets crawl across the rock as they feed, using a rough tongue-like part to scrape up a thin layer of algae. From above, a resting limpet may look like part of the rock.
facts: Some limpets press their shell down close to the rock when the tide is out, which helps keep moisture in.

title: How does a sea anemone catch food?
answer: A sea anemone can look like a flower, with a ring of soft tentacles around the center. It is an animal that eats other animals. Tiny cells on its tentacles can sting prey that brushes past. The tentacles help move food toward the mouth in the middle. Some anemones on rocky shores draw their soft parts inward when the tide goes out. Water covers it again when the tide comes in.
facts: Sea anemones and the tiny animals that build coral reefs belong to the same large group of animals.

title: What helps a sea star walk over rocks?
answer: Look under an arm of a sea star and you may see rows of short, soft parts called tube feet. Water inside a system of channels helps move the feet. One group of feet can attach while others reach for a new spot. Working together, they let the sea star creep across a rock. Some sea stars also use their feet to pull on the two halves of a mussel shell when they are feeding.
facts: A sea star is an animal without a backbone. It is not a fish.

title: How do California mussels stick to a rocky shore?
answer: A California mussel makes strong threads that fasten its shell to a rock or to other mussels. Waves can pull hard on the shell without sweeping it away. Many mussels end up packed together in a dark patch called a mussel bed. When covered with water, a mussel draws water through its body and catches tiny food in it. Taking food out of water this way is called filter feeding. If the rock becomes dry, the mussel can shut its two shells tightly.
facts: Small animals can shelter in the gaps between the shells of a mussel bed.

title: Why does a hermit crab borrow a shell?
answer: A hermit crab often carries an empty snail shell on its back. The shell helps cover the soft part of its body. If danger comes close, the crab can pull back into the shell. The shell itself does not grow with the hermit crab. As the crab grows, it may look for a roomier shell and move in when it finds one of the right shape and size.
facts: A hermit crab’s hard front legs stick out when it walks, while the softer back part stays inside.

title: Where do shore crabs hide when the tide goes out?
answer: A shore crab on a rocky coast may duck into a narrow crack or shelter beneath a rock as the water drops away. These spots can stay cool and damp while open rock dries in the sun. A crack can also hide the crab from animals that might eat it. Different kinds of shore crab use slightly different parts of the shore. A crab on the open rock can dart sideways to reach cover.
facts: Striped shore crabs on the Pacific coast often shelter in cracks in the rocks.

title: What lives in a tidal mudflat?
answer: At low tide, a wide stretch of soft mud may appear along a quiet coast. You might see holes, tiny trails, or birds poking their bills into the mud. Worms and some clams live below the surface, where the mud can stay damp until water covers it again. Wading birds can feed on those little animals. When the tide rises, some fish may come over the same flat to feed.
facts: Fine grains carried by water can settle where waves and currents are gentle.

title: Is a horseshoe crab really a crab?
answer: A horseshoe crab has a hard curved shell and a pointed tail. It belongs to a group more closely related to spiders than to true crabs. Its tail helps it turn over if it gets stuck upside down. On some coasts, adults crawl onto sandy beaches to lay and fertilize eggs. Shorebirds can eat exposed eggs, so a beach where the animals gather can also be an important stop for birds.
facts: The shell of a horseshoe crab helps protect legs that are hidden when you view the animal from above.

title: How does a barrier island shelter a coast?
answer: A barrier island is a long, usually narrow island that runs near and roughly along a coast. Ocean waves hit its outer beach first. On the sheltered side, there may be a quiet bay, mudflats, or marshes. Wind and waves can move sand from one side of an island to the other. A big storm may open a new gap where water can flow between the bay and ocean.
facts: A row of barrier islands can be broken by narrow waterways called inlets.

title: Who lives in the seaweed washed onto a beach?
answer: Waves often leave strips of seaweed and other natural material along a beach. This pile, called beach wrack, is food and shelter for small animals such as beach hoppers. Beach hoppers are tiny relatives of crabs that can jump away as you walk near them. Birds can feed on small animals in the pile. Wrack can gather along the highest part of the beach reached by a recent tide.
facts: A beach can have more than one wrack line left by water that reached different heights.

title: How can plants help protect a shoreline?
answer: On some quiet coasts, people use native marsh plants, sand, or oyster reefs to protect the edge between land and water. This is called a living shoreline. Plant roots help hold soil in place, and shallow plants or reefs can soften the push of small waves. Fish and crabs can still use the shallow edge to hide and find food. Planners choose which materials will work at each site.
facts: Living shorelines are most often used where the coast is sheltered from powerful ocean waves.

title: What makes a place a freshwater wetland?
answer: A freshwater wetland has water in or above the soil for long enough to shape which plants and animals can live there. Some wetlands have puddles you can see. In others the ground is soaked below a leafy surface. The water may come from rain, a nearby river, or groundwater rising from below the surface. Wetlands can give wildlife room to feed, and some hold extra water when nearby rivers rise.
facts: Not every wetland stays underwater throughout the year.

title: What grows in a freshwater marsh?
answer: A freshwater marsh often has shallow water and plants with soft stems. Cattails and some grasses grow with their roots in wet ground while their leaves stick into the air. Ducks and other birds can feed in open patches or hide among the stems. In a swamp, woody trees or shrubs are usually the plants that stand out. Both kinds of wetland can have deeper and shallower spots.
facts: Some freshwater marshes fill and drain with river tides even though their water is mostly fresh.

title: How can a forest grow in a swamp?
answer: Some trees can grow in ground that stays wet for much of the year. Where those trees grow together in a wetland, the place may be a forested swamp. A swamp floor can include shallow pools, wet mud, and raised spots around roots or fallen trees. The mix changes with the water level. The plants that grow there are often different from plants in a nearby drier forest.
facts: Bald cypress trees can grow in warm swamps in the southeastern United States.

title: How does a bog build up peat?
answer: In many bogs, rain and snow supply most of the water. Peat moss and other plants grow on top of a thick layer of soaked plant remains called peat. Old plant pieces break down slowly because the wet soil has little oxygen. More pieces get added on top over time. The water in many bogs is acidic and low in nutrients, so the plants that do well there can be quite different from those in a nearby forest.
facts: Some mosses in a bog keep growing at their tips while older parts below them slowly become peat.

title: What makes a fen different from a bog?
answer: A fen is a wetland that often builds up peat, just as a bog can. Much of its water comes from groundwater or from a nearby slope. That water can carry minerals it picked up as it passed through soil and rock. The minerals can make conditions in a fen different from those in a rain-fed bog. Some fens have sedges, which look a bit like grass, growing among low shrubs.
facts: A fen can be harder to spot than a pond because its water may be hidden below plants.

title: Why do some forest pools disappear in summer?
answer: A low spot in a forest can collect rain and melted snow and turn into a shallow pool. In some years that same spot dries up by summer. A temporary pool like this is called a vernal pool. A pool that dries regularly often has no fish living in it all year. That can give some salamanders and frogs a place to lay eggs with fewer animals likely to eat them.
facts: A vernal pool can be too dry to find in summer even though it was busy with life in spring.

title: Why does a spotted salamander visit a spring pool?
answer: Spotted salamanders spend much of their lives on land, often out of sight in damp woods. On rainy spring nights, adults may travel to temporary pools where their young can grow. The eggs sit in jelly-like masses in the water. Young salamanders hatch with gills and swim. As they grow, they change to a land-living form and can leave the pool, where the water may be drying up.
facts: A spotted salamander can live far enough from its pool that it needs a safe path between the woods and the water.

title: How did glaciers leave thousands of little wet places?
answer: Long ago, thick sheets of ice covered parts of what are now the northern United States and Canada. As the glaciers pulled back, they left many shallow dips across the land. Some dips collected water and formed little wetlands called prairie potholes. Some hold water for just part of the year. These pools are important places for ducks and other birds to raise their young.
facts: A prairie pothole can be surrounded by much drier grassland.

title: How does a bend in a river become a lake?
answer: As a winding river flows, it can wear away the outside banks of one bend. The two ends of that bend can slowly get closer. A flood or a change in the channel may let the river take a shorter route across the narrow strip of land. Mud and sand can close the ends of the old bend. What remains is a curved body of water called an oxbow lake.
facts: An oxbow lake may have the shape of a horseshoe or a wide letter U.

title: Why does a stream look rough in some spots and smooth in others?
answer: A shallow stretch of a stream can have rocks or gravel close to the surface. Water bumps over them and makes ripples. This kind of spot is called a stream riffle. In a nearby deeper pool, the water often moves more slowly and the top may look smooth. Both places give stream animals different options. Fish may rest in a pool, while small insects can hold onto rocks in the faster water.
facts: A stream can have many riffles and pools along just one short stretch.

title: Why do plants along a stream matter?
answer: The strip of plants beside a stream is called a riparian buffer. It can help both the land and the water. Tree roots help hold the bank together, and leafy branches shade the water. Grasses and other plants can slow rainwater flowing downhill, giving some of it time to soak in. Fallen leaves and bits of wood also help make places for small water animals to hide and feed. The plants form a living edge around the stream.
facts: Cold-water fish can depend on shade along streams that would otherwise warm too much in the sun.

title: Why do young freshwater mussels ride on fish?
answer: Many freshwater mussels start life as tiny young that spend time attached to a fish. The fish can carry them through the water while they develop. Later they drop away and settle on the bottom. As adults, mussels tend to remain in one small area, pulling water through their bodies to capture tiny bits of food. That is one kind of filter feeding. The fish ride helps young mussels spread away from where their parents live.
facts: Different kinds of freshwater mussel can need different kinds of fish for this part of their lives.

title: Why do so many pond plants grow at the edge?
answer: Near a pond’s edge, the water is often shallow enough for sunlight to reach the bottom. Some plants can put roots in the mud and send leaves up to the air. Others grow with floating leaves or stay completely under water. A thick group of plants offers insects and young fish places to hide. Out in deeper water, less light reaches the bottom, so a different set of living things may do well.
facts: Plants are not the only living things that use sunlight near the top of a pond. Tiny algae do too.

title: Can one lake have both warm and cold water?
answer: In summer, sunlight can warm the top of a deep lake while the bottom stays much colder. The warmer water near the top usually floats above the colder water. In many lakes, the difference between the layers shrinks in cooler weather. Wind can then mix water from close to the surface with water from deeper down. This mixing, called lake turnover, can happen at different times and to different depths from lake to lake.
facts: Shallow ponds can mix much more often than lakes that are deep enough to keep separate warm and cool layers.

title: What is a forest canopy?
answer: The highest branches and leaves of many trees together form a forest canopy. It is a kind of roof, with holes where light falls through. Leaves high up often get more sunlight than plants near the ground. Birds can nest on branches or feed on insects among the leaves. Wind can also reach that upper layer more strongly than it reaches the sheltered land below.
facts: A forest can have trees of several heights, so the canopy is rarely like a flat ceiling.

title: How do plants grow below a shady forest canopy?
answer: Shrubs, young trees, and some small plants grow below the tallest trees. This part of the forest is the understory. Less light usually reaches it than the canopy above. Some plants can make enough food in dim light. Others grow faster in small sunny spots. In some forests with trees that lose their leaves, wildflowers can get plenty of light early in spring, before new leaves spread overhead.
facts: Low shrubs can give birds a place to nest under the tallest branches.

title: What happens when a tall forest tree falls?
answer: When a tall tree falls, it can leave a hole in the forest canopy between the branches of its neighbors. Sunlight reaches more of the ground below that hole. Plants already growing there may grow faster. Seeds that need bright light may sprout. As years pass, the branches of nearby trees or the tops of new trees can fill the space again. While that happens, the fallen trunk creates a different home near the forest floor.
facts: Many small gaps can give a forest patches with young and old trees growing side by side.

title: How can a fallen log help the next forest grow?
answer: In some damp forests, a tree seed lands on an old log instead of reaching the soil. As the wood breaks down, it can hold moisture and give the seed roots a place to grow. The trunk that helps the seedling is called a nurse log. If young trees grow along the length of it, their trunks can form a row long after the original log is gone.
facts: As an old log crumbles away, roots that grew around it can leave little gaps below the trees they hold up.

title: Who lives in a dead tree that is still standing?
answer: A dead tree that has not fallen is called a forest snag. As some of its wood softens, a woodpecker may dig a hole to nest in. An old hole can later shelter a different bird or a small mammal. Tiny animals can hide in cracks or under loose bark. Standing dead trees eventually fall, changing from a high shelter into a log on the ground.
facts: A snag can be useful to wildlife even after it has lost most of its smaller branches.

title: What makes an old-growth forest special?
answer: An old-growth forest has had a long time to develop features that are often missing from younger forests. There may be very large old trees, smaller young ones, and trunks lying on the ground. Places where branches have opened up can let sunlight reach the ground. A single big tree does not tell you how old the whole forest is. Scientists look at several clues, and the features vary from region to region.
facts: Standing dead trunks and fallen logs can remain in some old-growth forests for many years.

title: Can a rain forest be cool?
answer: Some rain forests grow in places with cool or mild weather. In parts of the Pacific Northwest, moist ocean air brings heavy rain to the coast and mountains. Tall trees stand above thick moss, ferns, and fallen logs. Moss can even grow on the branches. A rain forest like this is called temperate because it grows outside the hot tropics. It can look much greener than nearby drier forests.
facts: The Hoh River valley in Washington state is home to a temperate rain forest.

title: Why does a tropical rain forest stay green?
answer: Tropical rain forests grow where the weather is warm and wet through much of the year. Trees there generally do not all drop their leaves in the same season. A tree can grow some new leaves while older ones fall, so the top of the forest stays green. Under the highest branches it can be quite shady. Vines and plants that live on branches can reach a brighter spot without growing a giant trunk.
facts: The tallest trees in some tropical rain forests stick up above most of the other trees.

title: Why does a deciduous forest change with the seasons?
answer: Many forests in places with cold winters have broad-leaved trees such as maples and oaks. These trees usually lose their leaves in fall and grow new ones in spring. That can make the forest floor much brighter before new leaves spread overhead. In summer those leaves cast shade again. Some other kinds of trees can lose their leaves during a dry season instead of a cold one.
facts: A tree that regularly loses all its leaves in one season is called deciduous.

title: How do trees live in the northern boreal forest?
answer: Across much of northern North America and Eurasia lies a great stretch of forest called the boreal forest, or taiga. Winters are long and cold there. Many trees are evergreens with narrow needles instead of wide, flat leaves. Keeping needles can let a tree start making food when warmer weather returns. Some boreal trees, such as larches, have needles but drop them for the winter.
facts: Many boreal forests include spruce or fir trees, but the mix changes from one region to another.

title: Why are forest edges different from the middle of a forest?
answer: Where woods meet a field, the trees are open to the sky on one side. There can be more sunlight and wind close to that edge than deeper among the trees. Dense shrubs can grow in the new light, and some birds prefer those shrubs. Other living things do better in the cool, sheltered forest interior. Cutting a big forest into small pieces usually makes more edge for the same amount of woodland.
facts: Some edges form naturally along rivers and open meadows.

title: What can happen when an old field is left to grow?
answer: Imagine a field that is no longer mowed. Tall grasses and small flowering plants may spread. Later, seedlings and shrubs can grow where their seeds land. Some may become trees that shade out the plants that first grew there. The change in the kinds of living things in a place over time is called ecological succession. Exactly what grows depends on the local weather, soil, seeds, and other changes in the land.
facts: A place that already has soil usually starts growing again differently from a bare surface of new rock.

title: Why can a grassland have so few trees?
answer: Grasses cover broad plains in places with a climate that can support them but often limits trees. The amount of rain is one part of the story. Fires, grazing animals, and dry seasons can also make it hard for trees to spread. Many grasses grow from buds low on the plant, where they can stay safe during grazing. Not all grasslands are alike, and trees may grow where water is easier to find.
facts: Temperate grasslands have several names around the world, including prairies and steppes.

title: Can prairie grass grow taller than a person?
answer: In some Midwestern prairies, grasses such as big bluestem can grow taller than a person by the end of summer. Their roots spread deep into the soil, helping the plants find water and return the next year. Wildflowers grow between clumps of grass. Fire and grazing can change how much of the prairie is tall at one time, so some patches can look very different from others.
facts: There can be more living plant material below the ground of a prairie than above it.

title: How do prairie plants grow back after a fire?
answer: In many tallgrass prairies, fires can burn dry stems without destroying every growing part of the grasses. Buds near or below the soil surface can survive and send up fresh shoots. Without fires, some shrubs and trees can spread into open grassland. The results depend on when the fire comes, how hot it gets, and which plants grow there. A prairie can have burned and unburned patches at the same time.
facts: Grazing animals may move toward a freshly burned patch to eat tender new growth.

title: How do savannas have trees and grass in the same place?
answer: A tropical savanna has grasses with trees or shrubs scattered among them. Many savannas have a rainy season followed by a dry one. Grass may cover the ground in the wetter months and dry out later. Fire and grazing can help keep young trees from filling every open space. Some trees survive and grow above the grass, making spots of shade for animals in the heat.
facts: Savannas occur on several continents. They do not all have the same trees or animals.

title: Can a desert be cold?
answer: A desert can be cold because what makes it a desert is the small amount of rain or snow it gets. Some deserts have very hot days, while others have winters well below freezing. In dry places, living things must get by with limited water. Some plants store water. Others grow and make seeds quickly when rain comes. The weather can change a lot across one desert, especially between high and low ground.
facts: A dry desert can have rocky hills, stony plains, or hard ground as well as sand.

title: How can a dry desert streambed suddenly fill with water?
answer: A desert wash is a channel where water can flow after rain. It might lie dry for much of the year. If a storm pours water onto nearby hills faster than the ground takes it in, the runoff can rush into the channel. The rain may fall far away from the place where the water shows up. The flow can move rocks and sand before the channel dries again.
facts: A wash may still be dry while a storm upstream is already filling it with moving water farther away.

title: How does a saguaro cactus keep water inside?
answer: Look at a saguaro and you can see long folds down its green stem. They let the stem swell when the cactus takes in water and draw in as it uses that stored water. Roots that spread out near the surface can pick up some water after a rain. The stem handles jobs that leaves do in many other plants, including making food with the help of sunlight.
facts: A saguaro grows in the Sonoran Desert, in parts of the southwestern United States and Mexico.

title: What can grow in Arctic tundra?
answer: Arctic tundra has a long cold winter and only a short time each year when plants can grow. Mosses, grasses, and low shrubs can spread close to the ground. In many places, part of the ground below the surface stays frozen even in summer. Tall trees have trouble growing in these conditions. During the short summer, the top layer of ground can thaw and make room for roots and small pools.
facts: Being close to the ground can help keep some tundra plants out of strong winds.

answer: Ground that stays at or below the freezing point of water for at least two years in a row is called permafrost. A layer above it can still thaw in warm weather and freeze again in winter. Some frozen ground contains a lot of ice. When that ice melts, the ground can settle and leave dips. Other permafrost contains very little ice. The word describes how long the ground stays that cold.
facts: Permafrost can occur in soil or rock. It does not have to be a solid piece of ice.

title: Why do trees stop growing high on some mountains?
answer: As you go up a high mountain, there may be a place where you stop seeing tall trees. This is the alpine treeline. Above it, the air is often cold and windy, and summers can be too short for most trees to grow tall. Low plants may still grow in sheltered places or near the ground. The height of a treeline changes with local weather and the shape of the mountain.
facts: Some trees just below the treeline are short and bent instead of straight and tall.

title: What do the arrows in a food chain show?
answer: Imagine grass, a rabbit that eats the grass, and a fox that eats the rabbit. In a food chain, an arrow leads from grass to rabbit, and the next leads from rabbit to fox. Each arrow shows the direction in which food and energy pass. The chain follows just one possible route. A real rabbit might eat several plants, and it might be food for more than one animal.
facts: In most food chains, a plant or another living thing that makes its own food is near the start. That living thing is called a primary producer.

title: Why do food chains make a web?
answer: A food web shows several paths that food takes through a place. Think of a pond where young insects eat algae. Small fish might eat those insects or tiny animals that drift in the water. A heron might catch a fish or a frog. If you draw an arrow from every food to the animal that eats it, you get a web of connections instead of a single chain.
facts: A food web can help you ask what other animals might be affected when one food becomes scarce.

title: How does sunlight get into a food chain?
answer: Green plants use energy from sunlight to make sugars from water and a gas in the air called carbon dioxide. A plant uses those sugars to grow. When an animal eats part of the plant, it gets some of the energy stored in the food. A plant is a primary producer because it makes its own food. Many tiny algae do a similar job in ponds and oceans.
facts: Some food chains deep in the ocean begin with living things that use energy from chemicals instead of sunlight.

title: Where do the materials in fallen leaves go?
answer: A tree drops a leaf into the leaf litter on the ground. Small animals can tear it into pieces. Fungi, bacteria, and other decomposers help break those pieces down. Some of the materials from the leaf enter the soil, where plant roots can take in some of them again. Other materials can leave as gases or move with water. Nutrients are materials living things use to grow, and some can be used over and over in an ecosystem.
facts: Leaves can break down faster in a warm, damp place than in a cold, dry one.

title: How can one kind of animal change a whole shore?
answer: On some rocky shores, sea stars eat mussels. If the sea stars disappear, mussels can take up more of the rock. That leaves less space where other animals or algae can live. A sea star can have a large effect even if it is only a small part of everything living there. Scientists call a species with an unusually large effect on its community a keystone species.
facts: The same animal can have a bigger effect in one habitat than it does in another.

title: Can an animal build places for other species to live?
answer: When a beaver builds a dam, water can spread behind it and form a pond. The pond changes how fast the water flows and which ground stays wet. Some animals that live in still or shallow water can use the new space. Other animals may do better in a fast stretch of stream. A beaver is called an ecosystem engineer because its work physically changes the places where many other living things can live.
facts: A pond made by a beaver can change again if the dam breaks or is no longer cared for.

title: What happens when a habitat is split into pieces?
answer: Picture a wide forest cut into smaller patches by roads and open fields. An animal that will not cross those spaces may reach only part of the forest it once used. A tree can stay in one place, but its seeds or pollen may have a harder time getting from one patch to another. The new forest edges can also be sunnier or windier than the old forest interior. This splitting into patches is called habitat fragmentation.
facts: Whether two patches feel cut off depends on the living thing. A bird and a ground beetle can cross different gaps.

title: Why can a city stay warmer than places nearby?
answer: On a sunny day, streets, roofs, and walls can warm up and hold some of that heat. At night they can release heat slowly, leaving some parts of a city warmer than greener places nearby. A neighborhood with many buildings and little shade can be hotter than a leafy part of the same city. Scientists call this pattern an urban heat island. Its size changes with the weather and the place.
facts: A grassy park and a parking lot only a short walk apart can feel different on the same afternoon.

title: How can a street tree cool a sidewalk?
answer: A tree’s leaves block some sunlight before it reaches the ground. A sidewalk under those leaves can stay cooler than a sidewalk in bright sun. Trees can also move water from their roots to their leaves and release it into the air as water vapor. That change uses some heat. A single tree has a small area of shade, but many trees can shade paths and buildings across a neighborhood.
facts: The shadow of a street tree moves during the day as the angle of sunlight changes.

title: Why do some buildings have plants on their roofs?
answer: Some roofs are built with a layer for plants to grow in above a waterproof roof. Leaves and the growing layer can catch part of a rain shower. Some of the water leaves again as vapor, and some can flow off more slowly. This can slow runoff. A roof like this can also shade the surface underneath its plants. The roof needs to be designed to hold the weight of plants and wet growing material.
facts: A green roof can slow rainwater but may still let water run off in a long or heavy storm.

title: How can a garden feed pollinators from spring to fall?
answer: One kind of flower may give bees food for only part of the year. A garden can grow several kinds of plants, with some that bloom early and others that flower in summer or fall. Local native plants often suit nearby pollinators, though the best choices depend on where the garden is. A small garden can provide a place for insects to stop and feed as they move across a neighborhood.
facts: Bees are not the only visitors. Some butterflies, flies, and beetles can move pollen too.

title: What makes a plant native to a place?
answer: A plant is native to a region when it occurs there naturally rather than arriving because people brought it from somewhere else. A plant native to one part of a country might not be native to another part. Local insects and other animals can depend on some native plants for food or shelter. A plant brought from another place is called introduced. An introduced plant can grow without necessarily becoming invasive.
facts: Some caterpillars can eat leaves from only a few kinds of plants, so the type of plant can matter as much as the number of plants.

title: Do some flowers get visitors at night?
answer: When many bees have stopped flying for the day, some moths and bats are just starting to look for food. A flower that opens at night may have a scent its visitors can follow. It may also have pale petals that are easier to see in dim light. As a visitor drinks nectar or brushes past the flower, it can carry pollen away to another flower of the same kind.
facts: Bright lights can change the routes of some night-flying insects and keep them away from flowers they might visit.

title: How can city lights affect birds flying at night?
answer: Some birds travel at night, when the air may be cooler. Bright lights from buildings can draw some flying birds toward lit areas, where they may get confused or fly into windows. The lights people use can change the way a night sky looks, especially when light shines up from the ground. Turning off lights that are not needed during migration can help reduce the problem.
facts: Many birds migrate, but some travel mainly during the day and others mainly at night.

title: Why might a bird fly into a window?
answer: A window sometimes acts like a mirror. A bird may see a reflection of tree branches or open sky and try to fly there. A bird can also fail to see clear glass when it looks through to plants on the other side. Patterns placed close together on the outside can help mark the window as a solid surface. A single mark may leave gaps that look like open space.
facts: Glass can reflect a backyard even when a person indoors can see through it.

title: How can people count the kinds of life in a park?
answer: During a bioblitz, people search one area for as many kinds of living things as they can find in a short time. One group might watch birds while another looks closely at plants. They record where and when they saw each kind. The list is a useful snapshot, but living things can be missed if they are hidden, active at night, or easier to spot in another season.
facts: A snapshot from one visit can be compared with later visits that use a similar method in the same place.

title: Why do cattails have brown heads that turn fluffy?
answer: A cattail’s tall brown head holds many tiny fruits that carry seeds. When the head breaks apart, they can drift off with a tuft of fine hairs. The hairs help the pieces catch air so wind can move them away from the parent plant. If a seed reaches wet ground with the right conditions, it can sprout. Cattails can also grow new shoots from spreading stems below the ground.
facts: A stand of cattails can spread both by sending seeds away and by growing new shoots close by.
